4 Experimental Setup
4.5 Evaluation Protocol
LLM-as-judge for post-training evaluation. All post-training numbers in this paper are produced by an offline evaluation judge that is implemented and run separately from the training-time reward judge (§3.7) and the training-time monitoring judge. These layers share neither a scoring scheme nor aggregation logic. Following Zheng et al. [33], the offline judge is DeepSeek-chat (DeepSeek-AI, dense) accessed through the DeepSeek cloud API. For each prediction, it emits a task-aware semantic relation label together with a continuous semantic score in [ 0, 1 ] ; this scalar is then thresholded to form a binary accuracy. For the single-cell cell-type task, we adopt a conservative operating point of τ = 0.8. Under this threshold, exact matches and strong ontology-consistent refinements are counted as correct, whereas broader lineage-adjacent or merely partially related predictions are not credited as fine-grained biological identification. For population tasks, the offline judge is applied at the per-cell level with task-specific prompt families (cell type, tissue, disease state), and per-cell scores are aggregated into sample-level summaries at a grain that depends on the reported metric (per-cellthresholded accuracy vs. per-sample mean-score correctness; see the Population evaluation paragraph below). Thresholds are task-dependent: we follow the operating points of τ = 0.75 for cell-type and tissue-type populations and the stricter τ = 0.85 for the disease-state population, consistent with the per-task figure captions in App. A.1-App. A.2.

Consequently, this separation spans multiple model-, serving-, and prompt-level axes rather than reusing the deployed judge stack from the RL phase. The intent is to reduce the risk of self-preference bias [52] in the reported metrics, not to establish formal statistical independence between the two judge stacks. 3

=== DOCUMENT ===
RVQ-Alpha: Bridging Single-Cell Transcriptomics and Large Language Models via Discrete Tokenization and Verifiable Reinforcement Learning
Guangpeng Li 1,2,† , Yue You 1,† , Yunlin Fu 1 , Weige Zhou 1,3 Feng Tang 1 , Jiaming Kong 4, ∗ , Luyi Tian 1,3, ∗
1 Guangzhou National Laboratory, Guangzhou, China 2 Electronic Information Engineering Program, School of Computer Science and Engineering, South China University of Technology, Guangzhou, China 3 GMU-GIBH Joint School of Life Sciences, Guangzhou Medical University, Guangzhou, China 4 Rectified Flow Capital Limited, Hong Kong SAR, China

--- CHUNK 10 ---
2 Related Work
2.4 Reasoning and Reinforcement Learning for Biological LLMs
Recent work has begun exploring reasoning-enhanced LLMs for single-cell biology.
CellReasoner [29] fine-tunes a 7B LLM with 380 chain-of-thought exemplars for marker-by-marker reasoning during cell-type annotation, thereby achieving strong few-shot performance.
Cell-o1 [30] applies reinforcement learning with batch-level rewards to single-cell reasoning puzzles, demonstrating a 73% improvement over OpenAI's o1 on batch-level annotation accuracy.
OmniCellAgent [41] employs multi-agent orchestration for autonomous single-cell analysis and hypothesis generation.
Beyond the single-cell domain, the RLVR paradigm has been applied to broader biological reasoning.
DeepSeek-R1 [32] demonstrated that verifiable rewards improve LLM reasoning by margins comparable to several months of pretraining scaling.
rbio1 [34] trains scientific reasoning LLMs using biological world models as 'soft verifiers,' setting the state of the art on the PerturbQA benchmark.
VCWorld [42] integrates structured biological knowledge with LLM reasoning for interpretable perturbation prediction.
RVQ-Alpha builds on these developments by combining discrete tokenization (enabling bidirectional generation), Evidence-First reasoning (grounding predictions in gene evidence), and RLVR with a Fact Verification module that validates claims against actual expression data. This integrated approach addresses the hallucination risk inherent in LLM-native biological tokenization.

--- CHUNK 11 ---
2 Related Work
2.5 Perturbation Prediction
Predicting cellular responses to perturbations is a core task for virtual cell models.
CPA [43] learns factorized perturbation embeddings with adversarial disentanglement.
GEARS [44] integrates gene-gene knowledge graphs for multigene perturbation prediction.
Diffusion-based approaches such as Squidiff [45] model perturbation responses through continuous denoising.
RVQ-Alpha addresses perturbation prediction through a distinct mechanism: RVQ tokens enable the model to autoregressively generate post-perturbation cell states, producing discrete token sequences that can be decoded back to expression profiles via the RVQ decoder.

--- CHUNK 12 ---
3 Method
RVQ-Alpha integrates four components into an end-to-end framework for single-cell transcriptomic reasoning: (i) a residual-quantization cell tokenizer that embeds gene expression into the native token vocabulary of the LLM (§3.2), (ii) a scCoT-Synth pipeline that constructs evidence-first chain-of-thought training data (§3.3), (iii) a three-stage training pipeline progressing from token grounding through multi-task SFT to reinforcement learning (§3.4), and (iv) a multi-teacher distillation and fact-aware reward system that unifies multi-task capabilities while suppressing biological hallucinations (§3.6-3.8). Figure 1 provides a system overview.
RVQ-Alpha: Bridging Single-Cell Transcriptomics and Large Language Models via Discrete Tokenization and Verifiable Reinforcement Learning

--- CHUNK 13 ---
3 Method
3.1 Problem Formulation
Inputs and outputs. Let x ∈ R G denote a single-cell gene expression profile with G ∈ [ 2,000, 36,602 ] measured genes, and let P = { x 1 , . . . , x N } ( N ∈ [ 10, 100 ] ) denote a cell population. Each sample is paired with an instruction t specifying the task. The target output y is either (i) a text response (such as a categorical label for cell type, tissue, or disease, a ranked gene list, or a CoT reasoning trace) or (ii) a sequence of RVQ discrete codes encoding a predicted post-perturbation expression profile.
Task families. RVQ-Alpha addresses seven task families spanning single-cell and population levels (Table 1).
Table 1: Task families supported by RVQ-Alpha. All single-cell tasks emit a CoT reasoning rationale alongside the answer.

Cell-type identification, Input = x , t. Cell-type identification, Output = Cell-type label. Cell-type identification, Level = Single-cell. Tissue identification, Input = x , t. Tissue identification, Output = Tissue label. Tissue identification, Level = Single-cell. Disease-state identifica- tion, Input = x , t. Disease-state identifica- tion, Output = Disease-state label. Disease-state identifica- tion, Level = Single-cell. Marker-gene identifica- tion, Input = x , t. Marker-gene identifica- tion, Output = Ranked gene list. Marker-gene identifica- tion, Level = Single-cell. Expression-profile gener- ation, Input = x , t. Expression-profile gener- ation, Output = RVQ-encoded expression profile. Expression-profile gener- ation, Level = Single-cell. Perturbation prediction, Input = P , t. Perturbation prediction, Output = Predicted post-treatment RVQ codes and implied differentially expressed genes. Perturbation prediction, Level = Population. Population comparison, Input = P , t. Population comparison, Output = Per-cell annotation and population-level summary. Population comparison, Level = Population
Three-stage optimization. Training proceeds through three stages with a composite objective:
<!-- formula-not-decoded -->
where L RVQ trains the cell tokenizer (§3.2), L SFT performs multi-task supervised fine-tuning (§3.4), and L RLVR applies reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (§3.7). Each stage builds strictly on the checkpoint produced by its predecessor.

--- CHUNK 18 ---
3 Method
3.3 scCoT-Synth: Evidence-Grounded Supervision Engine for Cold-Start RVQ Alignment
scCoT-Synth therefore comprises three generation tiers: (i) cell-level CoT generation across five annotation tasks (cell-type classification, tissue classification, disease classification, gene-name reconstruction, and expression-profile generation); (ii) population-level CoT across five tasks operating on groups of up to ∼ 50 cells; and (iii) audience-diversified continued pretraining drawn from a combinatorial space defined by four audience profiles, nine stylistic templates, and up to 108 variants along four content dimensions (analysis depth, reasoning path, gene organization, and data format).
All tiers share the core design principles of teacher scaffolding and conclusion-blind elicitation, adapted to the output format of each tier.
Multi-layer verification. Every generated trajectory passes through a verification stack spanning deterministic structural checks, rubric-based semantic scoring, and RVQ arithmetic validation (Table 2).
RVQ-Alpha: Bridging Single-Cell Transcriptomics and Large Language Models via Discrete Tokenization and Verifiable Reinforcement Learning
Table 2: Verification stack. Layers 1-5 are enforced during data construction; Layers 6-7 apply across all pipelines. † Non-blocking quality signal recorded with the CoT sample but never used to discard it. ‡ Blocking criterion for continued-pretraining samples; failures are regenerated by the teacher.

1, Name = Context constraint. 1, Method = System-prompt behavioral rule. 1, Enforcement = Soft †. 2, Name = Evidence-first structure. 2, Method = Regex position check. 2, Enforcement = Soft † / Hard ‡. 3, Name = Forbidden reference. 3, Method = Phrase filter. 3, Enforcement = Soft † / Hard ‡. 4, Name = Reasoning-conclusion. 4, Method = Regex label extraction. 4, Enforcement = Soft †. 5, Name = LLM-as-judge rubric. 5, Method = Weighted multi-dim rubric. 5, Enforcement = Soft (scored). 6, Name = RVQ code arithmetic. 6, Method = Offset + range validation. 6, Enforcement = Blocking criterion. 7, Name = Nomenclature norm.. 7, Method = Curated mapping rules. 7, Enforcement = Blocking criterion
The LLM-as-judge (Layer 5) evaluates CoT samples across four dimensions (evidence grounding, logic rigor, factual accuracy, and uncertainty calibration), utilizing a separate five-dimensional profile for continued-pretraining data. 2
This verification stack yields the final corpus of approximately 600K quality-assessed SFT samples across the 46 task variants.
Why it works: gradient pathway for cross-modal alignment. The evidence-first structure creates a gradient pathway from gene-name prediction positions back to RVQ embeddings via the attention value path:
<!-- formula-not-decoded -->
where AE indexes gene-evidence token positions and α i , j is the attention weight from position i to RVQ position j .
Within each layer, the gradient on e RVQ j is modulated by the attention mass assigned to that code at gene-prediction positions. This mechanism represents one of several gradient pathways that together provide a cross-modal supervisory signal without requiring an explicit mapping layer.
Ablation studies confirm this effect: removing evidence-first generation degrades accuracy by 8.3,pp and increases hallucinations from 4.2% to 23.7% (§6).

--- CHUNK 19 ---
3 Method
3.3 scCoT-Synth: Evidence-Grounded Supervision Engine for Cold-Start RVQ Alignment
The resulting corpus of evidence-grounded trajectories (comprising CoT chains and augmented narratives) provides the initial SFT supervision for cold-start RVQ alignment.
The structured output format, where gene evidence E precedes reasoning R , enables the downstream Fact-Aware RLVR module (§3.8) to decompose predictions into atomic biological claims for expressiongrounded reward verification.

--- CHUNK 20 ---
3 Method
3.4 Multi-Stage Training Pipeline
As noted in §3.3, the 256 RVQ tokens introduced by vocabulary expansion carry no pre-existing semantics in the language model: their embeddings are randomly initialized and bear no learned associations with existing representations in the model.
2 Reasoning profile weights: evidence grounding, = 0.30, logic rigor, = 0.35, factual accuracy, = 0.25, uncertainty calibration, = 0.10; each dimension is scored from 1 to 5 and normalized to [ 0, 100 ] .

Direct fine-tuning on task-specific data therefore faces a cold-start problem , because the model cannot extract meaningful information from RVQ inputs until these tokens are semantically grounded.
Even after grounding, supervised fine-tuning alone imposes a ceiling on output quality. The model can only reproduce reasoning patterns present in the training data and cannot self-correct factual or logical errors without outcome-based feedback.
These constraints motivate a three-stage pipeline (Figure 1).
Stage 1 (Continued Pretraining) grounds the new RVQ tokens in the representation space of the language model.
Stage 2 (Multi-Task SFT) teaches structured instruction following and CoT reasoning across seven single-cell task families.
Stage 3 (RLVR via GSPO) refines reasoning quality and factual reliability through verifiable reward signals (§3.7).
Across all three stages, the upstream RVQ encoder f enc remains frozen; only the LLM parameters are updated.

3.3 scCoT-Synth: Evidence-Grounded Supervision Engine for Cold-Start RVQ Alignment
scCoT-Synth therefore comprises three generation tiers: (i) cell-level CoT generation across five annotation tasks (cell-type classification, tissue classification, disease classification, gene-name reconstruction, and expression-profile generation); (ii) population-level CoT across five tasks operating on groups of up to ∼ 50 cells; and (iii) audience-diversified continued pretraining drawn from a combinatorial space defined by four audience profiles, nine stylistic templates, and up to 108 variants along four content dimensions (analysis depth, reasoning path, gene organization, and data format).
All tiers share the core design principles of teacher scaffolding and conclusion-blind elicitation, adapted to the output format of each tier.
Multi-layer verification. Every generated trajectory passes through a verification stack spanning deterministic structural checks, rubric-based semantic scoring, and RVQ arithmetic validation (Table 2).

Direct fine-tuning on task-specific data therefore faces a cold-start problem , because the model cannot extract meaningful information from RVQ inputs until these tokens are semantically grounded.
Even after grounding, supervised fine-tuning alone imposes a ceiling on output quality. The model can only reproduce reasoning patterns present in the training data and cannot self-correct factual or logical errors without outcome-based feedback.
These constraints motivate a three-stage pipeline (Figure 1).
Stage 1 (Continued Pretraining) grounds the new RVQ tokens in the representation space of the language model.
Stage 2 (Multi-Task SFT) teaches structured instruction following and CoT reasoning across seven single-cell task families.
Stage 3 (RLVR via GSPO) refines reasoning quality and factual reliability through verifiable reward signals (§3.7).
Across all three stages, the upstream RVQ encoder f enc remains frozen; only the LLM parameters are updated.

1 Introduction
We propose RVQ-Alpha , an end-to-end framework that resolves this challenge through three integrated innovations. Figure 1 illustrates the overall framework. Our core innovation is a Residual Vector Quantization (RVQ) autoencoder that compresses the expression profile of each cell into eight discrete tokens drawn from eight residual codebooks of 32 entries each (8 × 32 = 256 codes). This yields a variance-ordered decomposition that tracks cellular identity from broader lineage distinctions to finer functional states (a correspondence we validate empirically in §6), requiring approximately 60% fewer tokens than text-based representations. Because these tokens reside directly in the LLM vocabulary, the model can both interpret RVQ sequences for analytical tasks and generate new RVQ sequences for cell state simulation, thereby achieving bidirectional unification .

Bottom: The unified model drives diverse downstream applications, spanning single-cell, population, and perturbation analyses.

--- CHUNK 5 ---
1 Introduction
However, newly added RVQ tokens carry no biological semantics, creating a cold-start problem for this LLM-native integration scheme. To address this, we develop Evidence-First Feature-Injection SFT , which provides the topK expressed genes alongside RVQ tokens and enforces an evidencebefore-conclusion reasoning structure. This design forces the language modeling loss to align RVQ hidden states with gene-level semantics, using the training objective itself as an implicit alignment available under a CC-BY-NC-ND 4.0 International license. It is made bioRxiv preprint doi: https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.04.20.719773; this version posted April 23, 2026. The copyright holder for this preprint RVQ-Alpha: Bridging Single-Cell Transcriptomics and Large Language Models via Discrete Tokenization and Verifiable Reinforcement Learning signal. To further improve reasoning quality beyond what supervised learning alone can achieve, we construct a multi-component RLVR reward system [32] that evaluates answer accuracy via an LLM-as-judge approach [33] and assesses reasoning quality across five dimensions (independence, robustness, causality, granularity, and consistency). Furthermore, a Fact Verification module decomposes reasoning chains into atomic biological claims and validates each against the actual expression data of the cell. This expression-grounded verification extends the RLVR paradigm recently explored for biological reasoning [34] by providing fine-grained, cell-specific reward signals.
We evaluate RVQ-Alpha on a held-out pool of eight evaluation corpora curated from the ScBank singlecell collection (11,914 single-cell test samples spanning 12 tissues, five diseases, and 106 cell types), using disjoint training, validation, and test partitions (§4.5). Compared to supervised fine-tuning baselines, RLVR training yields consistent improvements: accuracy on the held-out immune-cell evaluation set improves from 70.7% to 82.8% (+12.1 pp), rare neuroblastoma recognition rises from 36.1% to 65.0% (+28.9 pp), population-level cell-type classification accuracy increases from 16.8% to 78.0% (+61.2 pp), and COVID-19 disease-state prediction accuracy doubles to 66.2%.
Our main contributions are as follows:

--- CHUNK 6 ---
1 Introduction
- We introduce RVQ discrete tokenization for single-cell transcriptomics, marking the first application of residual vector quantization to gene expression data. An eight-codebook residual quantizer (with 32 entries each) produces a representation of 10 tokens per cell embedded natively in the LLM vocabulary (§3.2), requiring 60% fewer tokens than text-based approaches (Table 8). Furthermore, empirical analysis (§6) demonstrates that earlier codebooks predominantly encode broader identity levels, whereas later codebooks refine within-lineage variation.
- We develop scCoT-Synth , an evidence-grounded supervision engine that overcomes the coldstart problem of newly added biological tokens without requiring a cross-modal projector. By coupling constraint-conditioned rationale synthesis with a seven-layer verification stack, this engine aligns discrete token representations with gene-level semantics entirely through the language modeling loss.
- We construct a multi-component RLVR reward system with Fact Verification that validates biological claims against actual expression data. This approach addresses the hallucination problem inherent in LLM-native biological tokenization, yielding up to a 4.6 × improvement on population-level tasks (Table 9).

Guangpeng Li 1,2,† , Yue You 1,† , Yunlin Fu 1 , Weige Zhou 1,3 Feng Tang 1 , Jiaming Kong 4, ∗ , Luyi Tian 1,3, ∗
1 Guangzhou National Laboratory, Guangzhou, China 2 Electronic Information Engineering Program, School of Computer Science and Engineering, South China University of Technology, Guangzhou, China 3 GMU-GIBH Joint School of Life Sciences, Guangzhou Medical University, Guangzhou, China 4 Rectified Flow Capital Limited, Hong Kong SAR, China

1 Introduction
We propose RVQ-Alpha , an end-to-end framework that resolves this challenge through three integrated innovations. Figure 1 illustrates the overall framework. Our core innovation is a Residual Vector Quantization (RVQ) autoencoder that compresses the expression profile of each cell into eight discrete tokens drawn from eight residual codebooks of 32 entries each (8 × 32 = 256 codes). This yields a variance-ordered decomposition that tracks cellular identity from broader lineage distinctions to finer functional states (a correspondence we validate empirically in §6), requiring approximately 60% fewer tokens than text-based representations. Because these tokens reside directly in the LLM vocabulary, the model can both interpret RVQ sequences for analytical tasks and generate new RVQ sequences for cell state simulation, thereby achieving bidirectional unification .
Figure 1: Overview of RVQ-Alpha. Top: An RVQ Encoder discretizes gene expressions, followed by a progressive Pretrain-SFT-RL alignment with an LLM to enable multi-modal reasoning. Bottom: The unified model drives diverse downstream applications, spanning single-cell, population, and perturbation analyses.

1 Introduction
However, newly added RVQ tokens carry no biological semantics, creating a cold-start problem for this LLM-native integration scheme. To address this, we develop Evidence-First Feature-Injection SFT , which provides the topK expressed genes alongside RVQ tokens and enforces an evidencebefore-conclusion reasoning structure. This design forces the language modeling loss to align RVQ hidden states with gene-level semantics, using the training objective itself as an implicit alignment available under a CC-BY-NC-ND 4.0 International license. To further improve reasoning quality beyond what supervised learning alone can achieve, we construct a multi-component RLVR reward system [32] that evaluates answer accuracy via an LLM-as-judge approach [33] and assesses reasoning quality across five dimensions (independence, robustness, causality, granularity, and consistency). Furthermore, a Fact Verification module decomposes reasoning chains into atomic biological claims and validates each against the actual expression data of the cell. This expression-grounded verification extends the RLVR paradigm recently explored for biological reasoning [34] by providing fine-grained, cell-specific reward signals.
We evaluate RVQ-Alpha on a held-out pool of eight evaluation corpora curated from the ScBank singlecell collection (11,914 single-cell test samples spanning 12 tissues, five diseases, and 106 cell types), using disjoint training, validation, and test partitions (§4.5). Compared to supervised fine-tuning baselines, RLVR training yields consistent improvements: accuracy on the held-out immune-cell evaluation set improves from 70.7% to 82.8% (+12.1 pp), rare neuroblastoma recognition rises from 36.1% to 65.0% (+28.9 pp), population-level cell-type classification accuracy increases from 16.8% to 78.0% (+61.2 pp), and COVID-19 disease-state prediction accuracy doubles to 66.2%.
Our main contributions are as follows:

1 Introduction
- We introduce RVQ discrete tokenization for single-cell transcriptomics, marking the first application of residual vector quantization to gene expression data. An eight-codebook residual quantizer (with 32 entries each) produces a representation of 10 tokens per cell embedded natively in the LLM vocabulary (§3.2), requiring 60% fewer tokens than text-based approaches (Table 8). Furthermore, empirical analysis (§6) demonstrates that earlier codebooks predominantly encode broader identity levels, whereas later codebooks refine within-lineage variation.
- We develop scCoT-Synth , an evidence-grounded supervision engine that overcomes the coldstart problem of newly added biological tokens without requiring a cross-modal projector. By coupling constraint-conditioned rationale synthesis with a seven-layer verification stack, this engine aligns discrete token representations with gene-level semantics entirely through the language modeling loss.

RVQ-Alpha: Bridging Single-Cell Transcriptomics and Large Language Models via Discrete Tokenization and Verifiable Reinforcement Learning
Guangpeng Li 1,2,† , Yue You 1,† , Yunlin Fu 1 , Weige Zhou 1,3 Feng Tang 1 , Jiaming Kong 4, ∗ , Luyi Tian 1,3, ∗
1 Guangzhou National Laboratory, Guangzhou, China 2 Electronic Information Engineering Program, School of Computer Science and Engineering, South China University of Technology, Guangzhou, China 3 GMU-GIBH Joint School of Life Sciences, Guangzhou Medical University, Guangzhou, China 4 Rectified Flow Capital Limited, Hong Kong SAR, China

RVQ-Alpha: Bridging Single-Cell Transcriptomics and Large Language Models via Discrete Tokenization and Verifiable Reinforcement Learning
Abstract
Integrating continuous single-cell gene expression profiles with discrete-token large language models (LLMs) remains an open challenge: text-based methods are token-inefficient and discard quantitative precision, continuous embeddings preclude autoregressive generation, and single-codebook vector quantization cannot stratify biological scales.
We present RVQ-Alpha , an end-to-end framework that bridges this modality gap through three contributions:
(i) a Residual Vector Quantization (RVQ) tokenizer that compresses each cell into a fixed 10-token sequence via eight residual codebooks embedded directly in the LLM vocabulary, requiring 3.4 × fewer tokens than prior discrete methods and enabling bidirectional unification of cell interpretation and generation;
(ii) scCoT-Synth , a teacher-student engine that grounds newly added biological tokens through evidence-before-conclusion reasoning, using the language modeling objective as the cross-modal alignment signal without a separate projection network;
and (iii) a Fact-Aware RLVR system combining an ontology-grounded answer judge with saliency-weighted verification of biological claims against actual expression data, under dynamic gating that conditions hallucination suppression on task competence.
Built on Qwen3-4B and trained via continued pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning, RVQ-Alpha substantially improves out-of-distribution generalization and rare-cell recognition across eight held-out datasets; ablations confirm that evidence-first grounding reduces hallucination more than fivefold.

1 Introduction
Building computational models that understand and simulate cellular behavior, a vision termed the AI Virtual Cell [1], is a central goal of computational biology. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) [2] provides the high-resolution transcriptomic data required by such models, and large language models (LLMs) offer powerful reasoning and generation capabilities that could serve as their computational substrate [3, 4]. Realizing this vision demands a model that can both interpret existing cell states (e.g., cell type annotation, disease classification) and generate new cell states (e.g., perturbation simulation) within a unified architecture. We address a specific setting: compressing continuous gene expression profiles into discrete tokens that reside directly in the LLM vocabulary, enabling a single autoregressive model to achieve both the understanding and generation of cellular representations.
This problem is particularly challenging because it requires simultaneously preserving quantitative expression information, achieving token efficiency, and enabling autoregressive generation through the LLM vocabulary.
Single-cell foundation models have scaled rapidly (from scGPT [5] with 33M cells and Geneformer [6] with 30M cells, to CellFM [7] with 100M cells and 800M parameters, and scPRINT-2 [8] with 350M cells across 16 organisms); yet, systematic benchmarks show that no single model dominates across all downstream tasks (Tables 8 and 9) [9, 10, 11]. More fundamentally, these continuous-representation methods [5, 6, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18] learn cell embeddings through masked expression prediction; they produce representations that enable accurate classification but cannot be decoded back through an LLM vocabulary . This architectural limitation precludes autoregressive cell generation and prevents integration with natural language reasoning chains.
To overcome this vocabulary incompatibility, text-based approaches convert expression profiles into natural language that pre-trained LLMs can process directly, using either ranked gene lists [19, 20, 21, 22, 23] or structured textual descriptions enriched with biological knowledge [24, 25, 26, 27]. However, these approaches introduce a different fundamental trade-off: ranked gene lists discard quantitative expression precision and produce token-inefficient representations (40-80 tokens per cell for the top-20 genes), whereas structured descriptions scale poorly to population-level multi-cell reasoning [28]. Recent work has further enhanced text-based LLMs with reasoning capabilities (for example, CellReasoner [29] introduces chain-of-thought annotation from 380 exemplars, and Cello1 [30] applies reinforcement learning with batch-level rewards). Nevertheless, these approaches still operate on text-based gene representations and lack mechanisms to verify biological claims against actual expression data .
A concurrent line of work explores discrete tokenization to resolve this trade-off. CellTok [31] demonstrates that vector-quantized variational autoencoder (VQ-VAE) discrete tokens, integrated into the Qwen2.5 vocabulary via early fusion, enable previously unattainable population-level analyses. However, CellTok employs a single shared codebook that cannot allocate capacity across biological scales; furthermore, it does not incorporate structured reasoning and relies solely on supervised fine-tuning without reinforcement learning. The core technical challenge remains: how to achieve discrete tokenization that preserves multi-scale biological structure, combined with verifiable reasoning that grounds predictions in actual gene expression evidence .

1 Introduction
We propose RVQ-Alpha , an end-to-end framework that resolves this challenge through three integrated innovations. Figure 1 illustrates the overall framework. Our core innovation is a Residual Vector Quantization (RVQ) autoencoder that compresses the expression profile of each cell into eight discrete tokens drawn from eight residual codebooks of 32 entries each (8 × 32 = 256 codes). This yields a variance-ordered decomposition that tracks cellular identity from broader lineage distinctions to finer functional states (a correspondence we validate empirically in §6), requiring approximately 60% fewer tokens than text-based representations. Because these tokens reside directly in the LLM vocabulary, the model can both interpret RVQ sequences for analytical tasks and generate new RVQ sequences for cell state simulation, thereby achieving bidirectional unification .

2 Related Work
2.4 Reasoning and Reinforcement Learning for Biological LLMs
Recent work has begun exploring reasoning-enhanced LLMs for single-cell biology.
CellReasoner [29] fine-tunes a 7B LLM with 380 chain-of-thought exemplars for marker-by-marker reasoning during cell-type annotation, thereby achieving strong few-shot performance.
Cell-o1 [30] applies reinforcement learning with batch-level rewards to single-cell reasoning puzzles, demonstrating a 73% improvement over OpenAI's o1 on batch-level annotation accuracy.
OmniCellAgent [41] employs multi-agent orchestration for autonomous single-cell analysis and hypothesis generation.
Beyond the single-cell domain, the RLVR paradigm has been applied to broader biological reasoning.
DeepSeek-R1 [32] demonstrated that verifiable rewards improve LLM reasoning by margins comparable to several months of pretraining scaling.
rbio1 [34] trains scientific reasoning LLMs using biological world models as 'soft verifiers,' setting the state of the art on the PerturbQA benchmark.
VCWorld [42] integrates structured biological knowledge with LLM reasoning for interpretable perturbation prediction.
RVQ-Alpha builds on these developments by combining discrete tokenization (enabling bidirectional generation), Evidence-First reasoning (grounding predictions in gene evidence), and RLVR with a Fact Verification module that validates claims against actual expression data. This integrated approach addresses the hallucination risk inherent in LLM-native biological tokenization.

2 Related Work
2.5 Perturbation Prediction
Predicting cellular responses to perturbations is a core task for virtual cell models.
CPA [43] learns factorized perturbation embeddings with adversarial disentanglement.
GEARS [44] integrates gene-gene knowledge graphs for multigene perturbation prediction.
Diffusion-based approaches such as Squidiff [45] model perturbation responses through continuous denoising.
RVQ-Alpha addresses perturbation prediction through a distinct mechanism: RVQ tokens enable the model to autoregressively generate post-perturbation cell states, producing discrete token sequences that can be decoded back to expression profiles via the RVQ decoder.

3 Method
RVQ-Alpha integrates four components into an end-to-end framework for single-cell transcriptomic reasoning: (i) a residual-quantization cell tokenizer that embeds gene expression into the native token vocabulary of the LLM (§3.2), (ii) a scCoT-Synth pipeline that constructs evidence-first chain-of-thought training data (§3.3), (iii) a three-stage training pipeline progressing from token grounding through multi-task SFT to reinforcement learning (§3.4), and (iv) a multi-teacher distillation and fact-aware reward system that unifies multi-task capabilities while suppressing biological hallucinations (§3.6-3.8). 3 Method
3.2 Residual Quantization for LLM-Native Cell Tokens
Tokenizing cell data for an LLM involves balancing competing requirements.
Aper-cell footprint short enough to fit tens of cells alongside instruction text in one context window demands aggressive compression, whereas preserving the continuum of cellular identity (from broad lineage distinctions to fine-grained functional states) requires expressive capacity.
Athird constraint compounds the first two: cell tokens must enter the LLM through its native token embedding table rather than through a separately learned cross-modal adapter, which would relegate gene expression to a secondary modality and add a trainable bottleneck between cell identity and the reasoning path.
Existing designs fail to optimally resolve this tradeoff.
Text-based encodings such as Cell2Sentence [19] consume 100-500 tokens per cell, thereby precluding population-scale prompts.

RVQ-Alpha addresses all three requirements with a residual-quantized tokenizer whose codes are embedded directly into the vocabulary of the LLM as a fixed representation of 10 tokens per cell.

Second, this variance-ordered decomposition permits, though does not guarantee, a correspondence with the hierarchical organization of cellular identity, where lineage typically dictates the primary axes of transcriptomic variation and functional states refine variation within lineages.

3 Method
3.3 scCoT-Synth: Evidence-Grounded Supervision Engine for Cold-Start RVQ Alignment
The 256 RVQ tokens introduced during vocabulary expansion carry no pretrained semantics. This cold-start grounding problem compounds the reasoning-format challenge of DeepSeek-R1 [32] with a cross-modal dimension.
scCoT-Synth addresses this issue by requiring every CoT training trajectory to decode RVQ codes into verifiable gene evidence before reasoning. Consequently, the standard next-token prediction loss forces the RVQ embeddings toward the gene-name representations already encoded in the pretrained weights.
The resulting engine produces approximately 600K training samples covering 46 task variants that span the seven task families.
Evidence-first constraint. Every CoT training sample follows a directed evidence-reasoning chain:

The model must produce verifiable gene evidence E (e.g., 'elevated CD8A , CD8B , GZMB ; absent CD4 ') before any reasoning step R .
Because gene-name tokens in E are predicted from RVQ input positions via the attention mechanism, the cross-entropy loss on these tokens provides a dense supervisory signal that pulls RVQ embeddings toward the pretrained gene-name representations, without requiring any explicit alignment module.
Scaffolded teacher-student synthesis. The constraint is realized through a teacher-student protocol with asymmetric information.
During teacher synthesis , a replaceable LLM backend receives curated gene features (such as expressionranked genes, known markers, active transcription factors, and functional gene modules) alongside c and t , enabling biologically accurate evidence-first reasoning.
A conclusion-blind elicitation protocol prevents the teacher from short-circuiting this process. Although the teacher receives metadata labels for context anchoring, the system prompt constrains it to derive conclusions solely from gene evidence, reasoning as if discovering them for the first time. Deterministic validators flag outputs that reference labels directly. For continued-pretraining data, the teacher regenerates these flagged samples; for CoT data, the flag is recorded as a non-blocking quality signal.
During student training , gene features are stripped entirely, and the input to the student contains only c ⊕ t .
Gene names survive solely in the assistant response (the training target) as evidence claims that the student must learn to predict from the RVQ codes alone.
The gene features thus act as scaffolding : they are present during construction to ensure teacher accuracy and absent during training to force genuine RVQ grounding.
Task-grounded generation at scale. Grounding RVQ tokens requires exposure across various biological granularities, including individual cell profiles, cell populations, and extended expository contexts, because a single granularity would bias the learned representations toward that specific level of description.

3 Method
3.3 scCoT-Synth: Evidence-Grounded Supervision Engine for Cold-Start RVQ Alignment
scCoT-Synth therefore comprises three generation tiers: (i) cell-level CoT generation across five annotation tasks (cell-type classification, tissue classification, disease classification, gene-name reconstruction, and expression-profile generation); (ii) population-level CoT across five tasks operating on groups of up to ∼ 50 cells; and (iii) audience-diversified continued pretraining drawn from a combinatorial space defined by four audience profiles, nine stylistic templates, and up to 108 variants along four content dimensions (analysis depth, reasoning path, gene organization, and data format).
All tiers share the core design principles of teacher scaffolding and conclusion-blind elicitation, adapted to the output format of each tier.

Direct fine-tuning on task-specific data therefore faces a cold-start problem , because the model cannot extract meaningful information from RVQ inputs until these tokens are semantically grounded.
Even after grounding, supervised fine-tuning alone imposes a ceiling on output quality. The model can only reproduce reasoning patterns present in the training data and cannot self-correct factual or logical errors without outcome-based feedback.
These constraints motivate a three-stage pipeline (Figure 1).
Stage 1 (Continued Pretraining) grounds the new RVQ tokens in the representation space of the language model.
Stage 2 (Multi-Task SFT) teaches structured instruction following and CoT reasoning across seven single-cell task families.
Stage 3 (RLVR via GSPO) refines reasoning quality and factual reliability through verifiable reward signals (§3.7).
Across all three stages, the upstream RVQ encoder f enc remains frozen; only the LLM parameters are updated.

3 Method
3.4 Multi-Stage Training Pipeline
Stage 1: Continued Pretraining
The goal is to ground the 256 newly introduced RVQ tokens in the pre-trained representation space of the language model prior to any task-specific supervision.
Vocabulary expansion adds five structural delimiters and 256 RVQ tokens. These are initialized under a diversity-promoting scheme ensuring that the new embeddings are geometrically dispersed rather than clustered in the representation space (full procedure in §3.2).
All parameters of the language model, including the newly added token embeddings, are jointly optimized under a standard next-token prediction objective.
The training data consists of RVQ-text paired descriptions spanning diverse linguistic registers (nine template families; §3.3), which are interleaved with biomedical literature and explicitly cover the top 500 gene names.
Unlike conventional continued pretraining with pure text, Stage 1 data already adopts an instructionresponse format. This enables task-oriented co-exposure : the model simultaneously learns RVQ semantics and the prompt structure of downstream tasks, thereby reducing the distributional gap to Stage 2.
The resulting checkpoint yields a model that maps RVQ tokens to meaningful representations but lacks structured task-following behavior, which motivates the multi-task supervision of Stage 2.

3 Method
3.4 Multi-Stage Training Pipeline
Stage 2: Multi-Task SFT
The goal of Stage 2 is to teach the model structured instruction following and chain-of-thought reasoning across seven single-cell task families.
The Stage 1 checkpoint is fine-tuned on the full scCoT-Synth corpus. Each training example carries a task-family annotation that selects the appropriate input formatting and loss masking for one of the seven task families.
Stage 2 performs full fine-tuning of the language-model backbone while keeping the upstream RVQ encoder frozen.
The loss is restricted to assistant token positions, ensuring that the model learns to generate responses rather than memorize prompts:

3 Method
3.4 Multi-Stage Training Pipeline
Stage 3: RLVR via Group Sequence Policy Optimization
The goal of Stage 3 is to refine reasoning quality and factual reliability beyond the SFT ceiling through reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards.
We adopt Group Sequence Policy Optimization (GSPO) [46], which operates at the sequence level rather than the token level (§3.5).
Its asymmetrically tight clipping bounds serve as the sole trust region, eliminating the need for an explicit KL penalty.
For each prompt q , the policy samples Ng candidate responses, each of which is scored by the composite reward signal (§3.7).
Rollout prompts are drawn from the same task families as in SFT, and group-normalized advantages (§3.5) provide a per-task baseline that adapts to heterogeneous reward distributions.
For multi-task scenarios, the Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD) protocol (§3.6) coordinates Stage 3 by first training task-specific experts through independent GSPO runs, and subsequently distilling their capabilities into a unified student.
The Stage 3 checkpoint constitutes the final RVQ-Alpha model evaluated in §4.

3 Method
3.6 MOPD: Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation
Motivation. Joint multi-task RLVR trained with a single mixed reward signal exhibits a persistent see-saw effect : reward gains on cell-type identification consistently degrade perturbation prediction accuracy, and vice versa. The root cause is gradient interference across heterogeneous task families whose reward landscapes are geometrically conflicting. Standard remedies are insufficient; mixedreward RLVR cannot simultaneously reach per-task peaks, and post-hoc parameter merging suffers from catastrophic forgetting. Inspired by MiMo-V2-Flash [48] and Baichuan-M3 [49], we introduce MOPD, a separate-then-unify protocol adapted for single-cell multi-task reasoning. Figure 3 provides empirical evidence for this design choice.

3.7 Ontology-Grounded Reward Design
Ontology-aware semantic evaluation. Exact-match rewards are ill-suited to biological cell type prediction, where valid names coexist at different levels of the Cell Ontology [50] hierarchy.
B cell' and naive B cell' are both correct descriptions of the same population at different specificity levels; T helper cell' and CD4-positive T cell' name the same entity in different nomenclatures.
Under exact-match scoring, a model that correctly identifies a naive B cell but outputs the parent term B cell' receives zero reward (identical to a prediction of neuron'), collapsing the entire ontological hierarchy into a binary signal that actively penalizes valid predictions.
The reward must therefore capture graded semantic similarity anchored to ontological distance, rather than reducing biological correctness to string identity.
Afrozen LLM judge addresses this by evaluating the semantic relationship between prediction ˆ y and ground truth y ∗ with explicit Cell Ontology awareness. The rubric below defines the reward-side answer judge , which is distinct from the post-training offline evaluation judge used to report accuracy (§4.5); its category schema and multi-sample aggregation are properties of the training-time reward system only.
The reward-side answer judge classifies responses into seven graded categories reflecting positions on the ontology graph, ranging from Exact Match and More Specific (valid sub-type) through Less Specific (valid ancestor) to Wrong Branch , Vague/Evasive , Wrong Lineage , and Unrelated , spanning a continuous score in [ -1, 1 ] (scoring intervals are detailed in Appendix A.4).
The overall reward pipeline is depicted in Figure 4.
Multiplicative gating. The continuous judge score is decomposed into positive and negative components, s + ans = max ( 0, s raw ) and s -ans = min ( 0, s raw ) , which enter the reward formula through disjoint paths.
Rather than a simple additive combination R = α R ans + β R reason, which allows a model to earn positive reward through plausible reasoning atop an incorrect answer, RVQ-Alpha employs a piecewise multiplicative gate :

where w base , w reason, and w neg are gating weights; P rule , P fmt , and P ans are non-positive penalty terms; and the final score is clamped to [ -1, 1 ] .
Three properties of this design are critical.
First, the hard gate : when the answer is wrong ( s + ans = 0), the reasoning score is entirely excluded; no amount of reasoning quality can compensate for an incorrect answer.
Second, the max ( 0, s reason ) clamp ensures that only genuinely constructive reasoning contributes a boost; neutral or negative reasoning yields zero rather than penalizing a correct answer.
Third, asymmetric penalty flow : the negative answer signal s -ans always propagates regardless of format validity, ensuring that the model cannot escape penalty by producing deliberately malformed output.
For population-level tasks, each of N cells receives an independent judge evaluation, and the positive and negative components are aggregated via the mean before entering the same gate (Eq. 19); population-specific consistency penalties and the aggregation formula are detailed in Appendix A.4.

3 Method
3.8 Fact-Aware Reinforcement Learning
The ontology-grounded reward described above ensures prediction correctness, but a correct answer produced through flawed reasoning (such as citing fabricated gene markers or hallucinating pathway associations) represents a distinct failure mode that the answer judge cannot detect.
Hallucination-accuracy trade-off. Standard hallucination-penalized RLVR using a count-based ratio R = R task + α · R hallu suffers from two failure modes: (i) redundancy-induced dilution , where the policy outputs many correct but uninformative sentences to inflate the denominator and suppress the apparent hallucination rate; and (ii) penalty-induced conservatism , where a large α drives the policy toward terse outputs that sacrifice the multi-step reasoning required for biological inference.
An effective fact reward must therefore weight claims by their informational importance to defeat dilution, while modulating its influence based on the current task competence of the model to avoid premature conservatism.
Inspired by Baichuan-M3 [49], RVQ-Alpha employs a saliency-weighted, dynamically gated factverification reward adapted for single-cell biological reasoning.
Saliency-weighted fact reward. Each reasoning chain is decomposed into independently verifiable atomic claims, which are evaluated against domain-specific knowledge bases covering cell-type markers, pathway memberships, and disease-gene associations, and subsequently classified as SUPPORTED, REFUTED, or UNCERTAIN.
Each representative claim c ∗ k is assigned a saliency weight that measures the maximum cosine similarity between its embedding and the embeddings of the response sentences. The weighted fact reward captures this variation in claim importance:

4.1 Base Model
RVQ-Alpha uses a single base LLM across all training stages and task families: Qwen3-4B-Thinking2507 [51] (4.0,B parameters, V text = 151,941), extended with Nc · C = 8 × 32 = 256 RVQ single-cell vocabulary slots, five structural delimiter tokens, and the top-500 gene name tokens (tokenizer details in §3.2).
The Thinking variant was selected because our RLVR objective explicitly rewards the reasoning trace (§3.7), aligning the native reasoning behavior of the model with the downstream training objective.

4.2 Training Protocol
Each step generates 128 trajectories (16 prompts × 8 rollouts) with a temperature of 1.0; training runs for 2,000 steps on eight GPUs with AdamW at a learning rate of 1 × 10 -6 (Table 4).
Unified Checkpoint Protocol. Each stage selects its output using the same protocol: saving periodically (every 1,000 steps for CPT and SFT, and every five RLVR optimizer updates for RLVR), scoring every saved checkpoint on a fixed held-out benchmark, and averaging the top-5 checkpoints by score with uniform weights (linear weight averaging in parameter space). The resulting merged checkpoint serves as the stage output from which the subsequent stage initializes and which is evaluated in this paper. The ranking metrics differ by stage: CPT and SFT use held-out single-cell LLM-judge accuracy, while RLVR uses task-specific LLM-judge accuracy on the per-task validation set.
All reported results use a single seed (seed 42). The checkpoint ranking uses stochastic one-sample decoding ( T = 0.6, topp = 0.95, topk = 20); individual scores therefore carry sampling noise that the top-5 merge attenuates. Donor disjointness between training and evaluation is strictly enforced for the homogeneous cell-type task and maintained as an operating convention for the remaining population tasks. The mixed-precision configuration (BF16 compute, FP32 gradient accumulation, FP32 AdamW moments) is summarized in the appendix. Full hyperparameter grids, the checkpointmerging configuration, the RLVR training hyperparameters, and prompt templates are deferred to the supplementary material.

LLM-as-judge for post-training evaluation. All post-training numbers in this paper are produced by an offline evaluation judge that is implemented and run separately from the training-time reward judge (§3.7) and the training-time monitoring judge. These layers share neither a scoring scheme nor aggregation logic. Following Zheng et al. [33], the offline judge is DeepSeek-chat (DeepSeek-AI, dense) accessed through the DeepSeek cloud API. For each prediction, it emits a task-aware semantic relation label together with a continuous semantic score in [ 0, 1 ] ; this scalar is then thresholded to form a binary accuracy. For the single-cell cell-type task, we adopt a conservative operating point of τ = 0.8. Under this threshold, exact matches and strong ontology-consistent refinements are counted as correct, whereas broader lineage-adjacent or merely partially related predictions are not credited as fine-grained biological identification. For population tasks, the offline judge is applied at the per-cell level with task-specific prompt families (cell type, tissue, disease state), and per-cell scores are aggregated into sample-level summaries at a grain that depends on the reported metric (per-cellthresholded accuracy vs. per-sample mean-score correctness; see the Population evaluation paragraph below). Thresholds are task-dependent: we follow the operating points of τ = 0.75 for cell-type and tissue-type populations and the stricter τ = 0.85 for the disease-state population, consistent with the per-task figure captions in App. A.1-App. A.2.

4.6 Baselines
RVQ-Alpha emits free-form natural-language cell-type labels end-to-end, graded by an LLM judge (§4.5). The primary numerical comparison is established through a two-layer rule. Protocol compatibility requires that a candidate produce a categorical label through its native, published inference protocol so that the same LLM judge can grade it without constructing a new benchmark bridge. Capacity fairness in the primary comparison additionally restricts that set to systems whose parameter scale is close enough to our 4B backbone for an accuracy gap to be interpretable as a method gap rather than a capacity gap. Three baselines satisfy both layers:
1. LangCell [24]: a Geneformer + PubMedBERT dual-encoder that performs zero-shot cell-type annotation via nearest-prototype scoring over cell-type names.
2. Cell-o1 [30]: a Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct model trained with SFT and GRPO that emits natural-language labels with reasoning chains.
3. C2S-Scale-Gemma2-2B [20]: a Gemma-2-2B model fine-tuned on cell sentences that emits a label string under the same text-generation protocol.
Other candidates anticipated by the single-cell community fall outside the primary comparison for diverse reasons rather than a single criterion. scGPT [5] and Geneformer [6] require an external protocol bridge before our judge can grade them; CellFM [7] requires task-specific fine-tuning for cell-type annotation; and C2S-Scale-Gemma2-27B [20] is protocol-compatible but, at 6.8 × the size of our backbone, falls outside the capacity-fairness layer and is therefore reported separately in §5.2 as a capacity-scaled reference rather than as a primary comparison point. App. A.6 documents the per-system rationale.

4 Experimental Setup
4.7 LCAD Computation
Computing LCAD (Eq. 24) requires mapping free-text predictions to Cell Ontology identifiers. We use the deterministic five-tier cascade summarized in §4.5; the only LLM-derived signal enters at Tier 4 and is bounded by a static lookup table whose maximum value is 6.0, so any reported LCAD > 6 originates from the ontology graph rather than the fallback. Across the eight evaluation datasets, the ontology graph (Tiers 1-3) resolves 49.6% of LCAD computations, with per-dataset coverage ranging from 22.6% on the lowest-coverage corpus to 84.1% on the highest, and leaves no unresolved predictions. The per-dataset breakdown and the full cascade specification appear in App. A.7.

Effect of defense mechanisms. The marker-stuffing defense resolves a reward-hacking pattern where the model over-specifies predictions with excessive gene markers; enabling it restores answer quality while maintaining a stable reward signal (Table 10, Notes (i)). 6.1 RVQ Compression Quality
Table 11 compares six configurations of the RVQ tokenizer on held-out cells, parameterized by the codebook count and the codebook size, denoted throughout this section as ( Nc , C ) . The chosen configuration, ( 8, 32 ) , achieves the best score on 7 of the 9 metrics: it minimizes MSE (0.0738) and MMD(0.0298), maximizes per-cell Pearson correlation (0.704) and ACS (0.708), and yields the highest scores across all three clustering metrics (ARI 0.247, AMI 0.557, NMI 0.589). It remains competitive on the other two metrics, ranking second in codebook usage (52.31%, trailing ( 32, 32 ) at 55.18%) and third in per-gene Pearson correlation (0.116).
Two configurations illustrate the failure modes avoided by ( 8, 32 ) . Wide-and-shallow codebooks ( 16, 512 ) underutilize capacity: only 9.81% of the 8,192 entries are actively used, leaving over 90% dormant. Narrow-and-deep sequences ( 128, 8 ) , conversely, suffer uniform degradation across all reconstruction metrics (PCC c drops to 0.652, ACS drops to 0.661, MMD rises to 0.0388) without providing any clustering benefits. Thus, ( 8, 32 ) combines optimal reconstruction and clustering quality with a minimal footprint on the LLM side (only 256 added vocabulary entries and 8 tokens per cell), making it the standard configuration for the remainder of RVQ-Alpha.

6 Analysis
6.2 Semantic Understanding of RVQ Tokens
Evidence for the hierarchy hypothesis. Section 3.2 hypothesizes that the variance-ordered decomposition produced by residual quantization exhibits a coarse-to-fine correspondence with the hierarchical organization of cellular identity. Figure 8 supports this hypothesis: a directed-graph analysis over 100K class-balanced cells shows that earlier codebooks (CB-0-CB-2) predominantly partition cells at broader identity levels (major cell groups, representative subtypes, shared cell states), whereas later codebooks (CB-3-CB-4) refine within-lineage variation into functional programs and pathway markers. We note that this serves as evidence rather than formal proof; the decomposition allows, but does not guarantee, such an alignment, as residual codebooks are trained symmetrically.
Semantic structure of predictions. To assess whether the LLM develops a biological understanding of RVQtokens rather than merely memorizing mappings, we examine the semantic confusion structure of its predictions alongside the corresponding embedding-space organization in Appendix A.1 (Figures 10 and 11). The confusion matrix shows that most off-diagonal mass concentrates between ontologically adjacent cell types rather than across unrelated lineages, confirming that RVQ tokenization preserves the local semantic structure of gene expression. The companion t-SNE visualization shows that biologically related cell types cluster together in the RVQ embedding space of the LLM. Neuronal cells form a distinct cluster separated from immune and epithelial lineages, while immune subtypes (T cells, NK, Myeloid) exhibit substantial overlap, which is consistent with their shared ontological proximity. Based on these complementary views, we hypothesize three properties regarding the underlying interaction between RVQ and reasoning: (1) attention over RVQ positions tracks biologically relevant gene modules; (2) attention shifts across codebook positions depending on the biological property the model evaluates (lineage versus functional state); and (3) codebook combinations unseen during training continue to yield biologically coherent predictions. We state these explicitly as hypotheses, leaving direct evidence from attention patterns to future work. Companion confusion matrices for tissue type and disease state, along with an alluvial diagram of misclassification flows, are provided in the same appendix (Figures 12-14).

The two hard gates, A ′ and A ′′ , eliminate three reward-hacking modes that emerged during training (marker stuffing, template regurgitation, and multi-pattern over-specification), which are documented in Table 10.

Deciphering  the  mapping  between  linear  biomolecular  sequences  and  complex  biological  functions remains a central challenge in genomics. Although existing generative nucleotide language models have made substantial progress  in  modeling  sequence  distributions,  they  generally  lack  explicit  access  to high-level biological semantics, limiting their ability to support semantics-guided conditional generation. GenNA: Conditional generation of nucleotide sequences guided by natural-language annotations
Main
Understanding how nucleotide sequences encode complex biological functions has long been a central question  in  genomics  and  synthetic  biology 1 .  In  recent  years,  the  rapid  development  of  foundation models  for  protein  and  nucleic  acid  sequence  modeling  has  transformed  the  view  that  biological sequences  can  be  treated  as  a  learnable  language  from  a  conceptual  analogy  into  an  operational computational paradigm 2 .  In  the  protein  domain  in  particular,  large-scale  self-supervised learning has shown that models can acquire representations associated with structure, fitness, and function purely from sequence statistics 3,4 . This progress has, in turn, directly motivated the extension of language-modeling approaches to DNA and RNA sequences.
Nucleotide  foundation  models  have  advanced  along  several  related  but  distinct  trajectories.  For nucleotide  sequence  representation  and  prediction,  encoder-based  models  such  as  DNABERT 5 and Nucleotide Transformer 6 have  been  followed  by  longer-context  and  sequence-to-function  frameworks including  DNABERT-2 7 ,  GENA-LM 8 ,  AlphaGenome 9 and  Nucleotide  Transformer  v3 10 ,  collectively showing that large-scale pretraining can capture regulatory, mutational and cross-species signals across increasingly long genomic  contexts.  For  sequence  generation,  autoregressive  models  such  as GenSLMs 11 , DNAGPT 12 and HyenaDNA 13 , followed by later genome-scale models including megaDNA 14 , Evo 15 ,  Evo 2 16 ,  GENErator 17 and ATGC-Gen 18 ,  have demonstrated that nucleotide sequences can be modeled and designed directly within generative frameworks.
However,  the  explicit  use  of  natural-language  annotations  as  the  primary  conditioning  signal  for nucleotide  sequence  generation  remains  comparatively  underexplored.  Previous  approaches  rely  on structured  labels  or  predefined  attributes,  whose  limited  expressivity  struggles  to  capture  complex, context-dependent  biological  functions.  In  contrast,  natural  language  provides  a  vastly  more  flexible representation, more suitable for expressing human intent. In the absence of effective mechanisms to integrate such  rich and heterogeneous information,  most generative models rely mainly on sequence prefixes, local context, or specific structured attributes for conditional modeling. Even OmniNA 19 , despite jointly modeling nucleotide sequences and textual annotations, mainly emphasizes sequence-to-annotation  generation  and  sequence  understanding  rather  than  annotation-conditioned sequence design.

GenNA: Conditional generation of nucleotide sequences guided by natural-language annotations
Results
Architecture and pretraining of the GenNA foundation model
GenNA  is  a decoder-only generative foundation model  for nucleotide sequences.  Its network configuration  follows  the  Qwen3  Transformer 22 design  paradigm,  and  the  model  was  pretrained  from scratch using a custom cross-modal vocabulary, resulting in approximately 3.6 billion parameters (Fig. 1a). Unlike nucleotide models that are primarily based on masked language modeling 24 , GenNA adopts an autoregressive framework to enable direct sequence generation. Building on this framework, GenNA incorporates natural-language prompts at the beginning of the sequence to provide biological information. This  design  extends  the  conditioning  space  of  autoregressive  generation  by  incorporating  high-level biological semantics, including species identity, gene names and functional annotations, alongside local sequence context.
The pretraining data were derived from the NCBI RefSeq database 25 . After curation, we constructed a multimodal corpus covering 2,221 eukaryotic species and totaling approximately 416 billion characters (Fig.  1b-d  and  Supplementary  Table  1).  In  addition  to  nucleotide  sequences  from  gene-associated regions,  the  corpus  incorporates  natural-language  functional  metadata  and  XML-style  structured annotations  (Supplementary  Table  2).  To  handle  this  heterogeneous  data  type,  we  further  trained  a unified  cross-modal  BPE  tokenizer 23 ,  allowing  frequent  functional  phrases,  tag  fragments,  and  local nucleotide patterns to be mapped into a shared discrete token space (Fig. 1e-h). This facilitates the joint modeling of sequence patterns, functional semantics and structural boundary information within a unified representation space.
During training, we used a causal language modeling objective 20 , in which the model predicts the next token conditioned on the preceding context. GenNA was pretrained from scratch on a computing cluster composed  of  multiple  NVIDIA  A800  GPUs,  with  a  maximum  context  length  of  4,096  tokens, available under a CC-BY 4.0 International license. GenNA internalizes sequence-function relationships
The pretraining corpus contains a large number of paired nucleotide sequences and natural-language functional annotations, suggesting that the model may capture relationships between sequence patterns and functional semantics. To evaluate whether GenNA is genuinely sensitive to the consistency between sequences  and  their  functional  annotations,  we  first  assessed  its  response  to  sequence-function mismatches  using  perplexity  (PPL)  and  then  examined  attention  scores  in  intermediate  Transformer layers to assess how natural-language prompts contribute to autoregressive nucleotide generation.
While keeping the underlying nucleotide sequence completely unchanged, we systematically replaced the  functional  annotation  in  the  input  prompt.  The  results  showed  that,  when  the  natural-language functional  annotation  was  mismatched  with  the  corresponding  sequence,  the  model's  average  PPL increased substantially  (Fig.  2a,b).  In  addition,  gene-annotation swapping  across  15  genes  from  four families produced a structured Δ PPL pattern, suggesting that the model captures family-level functional relatedness (Supplementary Fig. 4).This elevated uncertainty in response to semantically inconsistent inputs  indicates  that  GenNA  does  not  rely  solely  on  local  nucleotide  context  but  instead  jointly incorporates functional-semantic information provided by the prompt.
To further investigate this phenomenon at the level of internal representations, we analyzed the token level attention scores in Transformer layer 18 27 . Using the Spodoptera litura glutaminase liver isoform, mitochondrial isoform X1 for example, we observed that even when the generation position was distant from the prompt region, the model continued to attend to functional annotations and structural labels throughout the generation process (Fig. 2c). Across 100 randomly sampled sequences, we observed that during coding sequence (CDS) generation, prompt tokens accounted for an average of 64.4% of the attention weight, whereas relatively less attention was assigned to the upstream 5' UTR (Fig. 2d). This pattern  is  consistent  with  the  interpretation  that  prompt  tokens  continue  to  provide  conditioning constraints throughout the generation process. Prompt ablation further supported the interpretation that functional annotation provides the dominant semantic signal (Supplementary Fig. 3).
Taken  together,  these  results  indicate  that  GenNA  captures  relationships  between  natural-language functional annotations and nucleotide sequences. Results
Zero-shot prediction of mutation effects
To  evaluate  the  sensitivity  of  GenNA  to  single-nucleotide  perturbations  in  functional  sequences,  we performed in silico mutational scanning on protein-coding genes and compared the perplexity changes induced by different mutation types (Fig. 2e,f). Within the evaluation framework used in this study, Δ PPL can  be  interpreted  as  the  model's  response  how  far  a  mutated  sequence  deviates  from  the  natural distribution 28,29 . It therefore provides a useful proxy for comparing the relative impact of different classes of perturbations on the model's internal assessment of sequence function.
Δ These  results  show  that,  even  without  any  task-specific  fine-tuning  on  variant  data,  GenNA  displays discriminative responses to different classes of mutations solely as a result of large-scale pretraining, consistent with findings in other genomic foundation models 6 . The Δ PPL used here reflects changes in model likelihood induced by perturbations that deviate from the learned distribution of natural sequences, and is therefore treated as a quantitative proxy for mutation-induced deviations in sequence likelihood rather than a direct experimental measurement of phenotypic effects. Nevertheless, the emergence of this stratified pattern in the absence of population-level variation data from the same species suggests that  cross-species  pretraining  can  endow  the  model  with  sensitivity  to  coding  constraints  and  local sequence abnormalities.
The results revealed a clearly stratified pattern across mutation categories. In general, single-nucleotide mutations occurring in non-coding regions (such as 3 ′ and 5 ′ UTR substitutions or deletions), as well as synonymous substitutions  within  the  coding sequence (CDS), caused only  modest changes  in Δ PPL (median values ranging from -0.015 to 0.076). This suggests that the model is relatively tolerant of local perturbations that do not alter the encoded product (Fig. 2e). By contrast, when a mutation changed the amino acid composition or disrupted the reading frame, the model exhibited a much stronger rejection signal. The median Δ PPL associated with missense mutations (0.291) was approximately four-fold higher than that of synonymous mutations (0.076), indicating that the model can distinguish simple nucleotide substitutions from coding changes that are more likely to affect the protein product. For more disruptive mutation types, the increase in perplexity was even more pronounced. Nonsense mutations introducing premature stop codons resulted in a substantial median Δ PPL of 1.732. Stop-loss mutations disrupting the  original  termination  codon  also  showed  comparable  increases  (median Δ PPL  =  1.558),  while single-base deletions causing frameshifts produced the strongest overall effect by a wide margin (median PPL = 5.411) (Fig. 2e,f). This overall trend is highly consistent with the degree to which coding-region integrity is compromised.

Results
Broad and meaningful sequence generation
One  of  the  central  goals  of  GenNA  is  to  enable  conditional  nucleotide  generation  guided  by natural-language annotations. To evaluate whether the generated outputs are not only formally plausible but  also  consistent  with  the  underlying  biological  context  in  both  semantic  and  statistical  terms,  we systematically analyzed model behavior across multiple generation settings (Fig. 3a).
We first evaluated unconditional generation under highly minimal conditions. In this setting, all explicit constraints were removed, and the model was provided only with a modality tag (Genomic DNA or RNA). It was then required to autoregressively generate the complete metadata fields, including species, gene name, and functional  annotation,  followed  by  the  corresponding  nucleotide  sequence.  For  generated mRNA sequences, we extracted the CDS regions and translated them into protein sequences, which were then aligned against existing databases using BLASTP 33 . We subsequently used Sentence-Transformers 34 to evaluate the semantic consistency between the model-generated functional annotations and the annotations associated with the top database hits. Sequence-logo analysis of these unconditionally generated mRNAs further recovered a Kozak-like translation-initiation context, which is a meaningful  local  sequence  grammar  (Supplementary Fig.  5).  The  results  showed  that  the  generated annotations remained well aligned with the corresponding generated sequences at the semantic level (Fig. 3b).
We  next  evaluated  species-specific  generation  to  investigate  whether  the  model  could  leverage species-specific  properties  to guide sequence  generation. Without  imposing  any  explicit constraint  on gene function, we prompted the model to generate nucleotide sequences from six representative model organisms:  human (Homo  sapiens) ,  zebrafish (Danio  rerio) , fruit fly (Drosophila  melanogaster) , Arabidopsis  thaliana ,  yeast (Saccharomyces  cerevisiae) ,  and  maize (Zea  mays) . In addition to preserving semantic self-consistency (Fig. 3c), GenNA successfully reproduced species-specific features in  the  generated  sequences  (Fig.  3d-g).  For  example,  the  GC-content  distributions  of  the  generated sequences were broadly consistent with those of the corresponding reference genomes, and the model captured systematic differences across species ranging from relatively low-GC to high-GC backgrounds. Similar trends were also observed for GC3, codon-usage bias, and amino acid frequency.
In addition, we observed that the generated distributions were more concentrated than the corresponding natural reference distributions, exhibiting a degree of distribution sharpening. In fruit fly and maize, for example, the generated sequences tended to cluster more strongly around the most representative GC ranges  of  each  species,  whereas  coverage  of  the  long-tail  regions  in  the  natural  distributions  was relatively limited (Fig. 3e). GenNA: Conditional generation of nucleotide sequences guided by natural-language annotations
Discussion
In this study, we introduced GenNA, a generative large language model for nucleotide sequences guided by natural-language annotations. Unlike prior approaches that are primarily designed to model a single sequence modality, GenNA employs a dedicated cross-modal BPE vocabulary and joint pretraining on large-scale eukaryotic genomic and transcriptomic corpora to establish associations between functional semantics and sequence syntax within a unified autoregressive framework. Our results show that this training strategy not only enables the model to capture the intrinsic patterns of nucleotide sequences themselves, but also allows it to leverage natural-language functional annotations and species context for consistency evaluation and conditional generation over entire conditioned inputs.
GenNA  exhibits  several  notable  emergent  properties  at  multiple  levels.  First,  in  in  silico  mutational scanning, the model shows a stratified perplexity response across synonymous, missense, nonsense, and  frameshift  mutations,  with  more  disruptive  variants  generally  associated  with  larger Δ PPL.  This pattern suggests that the model has learned statistical features related to genetic-code degeneracy and coding-sequence  integrity.  Second,  even  without  explicit  supervision  from  a  taxonomic  tree,  both  the intermediate-layer representations of GenNA and the Δ PPL matrix derived from species-label swapping reveal a degree of species-associated structure, indicating that cross-species pretraining may enable the model to capture phylogeny-related latent similarities 30 . GenNA used a decoder-only Transformer architecture. Its core network configuration was based on the

GenNA: Conditional generation of nucleotide sequences guided by natural-language annotations
Main
Understanding how nucleotide sequences encode complex biological functions has long been a central question  in  genomics  and  synthetic  biology 1 .  In  recent  years,  the  rapid  development  of  foundation models  for  protein  and  nucleic  acid  sequence  modeling  has  transformed  the  view  that  biological sequences  can  be  treated  as  a  learnable  language  from  a  conceptual  analogy  into  an  operational computational paradigm 2 .  In  the  protein  domain  in  particular,  large-scale  self-supervised learning has shown that models can acquire representations associated with structure, fitness, and function purely from sequence statistics 3,4 . This progress has, in turn, directly motivated the extension of language-modeling approaches to DNA and RNA sequences.
Nucleotide  foundation  models  have  advanced  along  several  related  but  distinct  trajectories.  For nucleotide  sequence  representation  and  prediction,  encoder-based  models  such  as  DNABERT 5 and Nucleotide Transformer 6 have  been  followed  by  longer-context  and  sequence-to-function  frameworks including  DNABERT-2 7 ,  GENA-LM 8 ,  AlphaGenome 9 and  Nucleotide  Transformer  v3 10 ,  collectively showing that large-scale pretraining can capture regulatory, mutational and cross-species signals across increasingly long genomic  contexts.  For  sequence  generation,  autoregressive  models  such  as GenSLMs 11 , DNAGPT 12 and HyenaDNA 13 , followed by later genome-scale models including megaDNA 14 , Evo 15 ,  Evo 2 16 ,  GENErator 17 and ATGC-Gen 18 ,  have demonstrated that nucleotide sequences can be modeled and designed directly within generative frameworks.
However,  the  explicit  use  of  natural-language  annotations  as  the  primary  conditioning  signal  for nucleotide  sequence  generation  remains  comparatively  underexplored.  Previous  approaches  rely  on structured  labels  or  predefined  attributes,  whose  limited  expressivity  struggles  to  capture  complex, context-dependent  biological  functions.  In  contrast,  natural  language  provides  a  vastly  more  flexible representation, more suitable for expressing human intent. In the absence of effective mechanisms to integrate such  rich and heterogeneous information,  most generative models rely mainly on sequence prefixes, local context, or specific structured attributes for conditional modeling. Even OmniNA 19 , despite jointly modeling nucleotide sequences and textual annotations, mainly emphasizes sequence-to-annotation  generation  and  sequence  understanding  rather  than  annotation-conditioned sequence design.
Against  this  backdrop,  we  present  GenNA,  a  generative  nucleotide  foundation  model  guided  by natural-language  annotations.
